extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media scholars, and news professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria used by journalists and news organizations when selecting, editing, and presenting stories for mass audiences, including audience-segmentation, content restrictions (taste), and strategies to attract or protect audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional news judgment / editorial autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists believe they must "give the audience what it needs, not what it wants" and that "you can't edit by readership survey, so we have to take the lead." They privilege professional intuition and news judgment over formal audience feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard justifies resisting audience surveys or letters when they conflict with editors' sense of importance; journalists assume their professional role entitles them to act as delegates of the audience. Anti-pattern: surrendering story selection to simple readership metrics or momentary audience taste at the expense of perceived public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of informal / known-audience feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary feedback is often informal and self-generated: from superiors, family, friends, neighbors, and colleagues (the 'known audience' or 'near-audience').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists commonly test material on office staff, spouses, neighbors, or colleagues who adopt a lay role. This is treated as representative enough by practitioners, though the text notes this assumption is inaccurate. Example: testing photos or headlines on staff members before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generated feedback from the unknown audience (audience hunger)
rubrics_metrics.description: When informal feedback is insufficient, journalists may provoke measurable audience reaction by selecting stories guaranteed to elicit calls or letters (e.g., risqué pieces, human-interest items that inspire donations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a deliberate tactic to learn whether 'anyone out there' is watching; it can skew editorial selection toward stories engineered to produce response rather than to inform. Example: choosing a human-interest segment sure to trigger letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-image segmentation (interested, uninterested, rejected, invented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists construct images of their audience and divide it into types: the interested (regular, engaged), the uninterested (irregular, hold attention with 'crumbs'), the rejected (e.g., would-be intellectuals or sensationalists), and the invented (audiences journalists assume exist to justify choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story selection is adjusted according to which imagined segment is being served. For the uninterested, journalists aim to attract and hold attention; for the interested, they may preserve analytical depth. Warning: these images often overestimate the educated/upscale audience and do not accurately represent the full demographic reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying stories (attracting: identification & action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select stories that enable audience identification — personal relevance, action, clear hero/villain/victim dynamics — and that are 'memorable' enough to be discussed and generate word-of-mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action and human-centered narratives are seen as inherently engaging. Example: Reuven Frank's goal to 'irritate' viewers (i.e., get them involved). Usefulness: increases attention and possible audience growth. Anti-pattern: choosing abstract or purely analytic pieces that few can identify with, unless targeted to the 'interested' audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service stories (attracting: personal relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include service journalism — information of direct personal relevance such as health, consumer guidance, or clear periodic summaries of complex phenomena — even if editors find them dull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stories 'service our confused readers' and are chosen to fulfill a duty to inform practical needs. Example: Newsweek's reviews of CIA investigations or campaign funding regulations. Note: journalists may produce these reluctantly but consider them necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-burdening presentation (clarity / avoid excessive detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overburdening the audience with complicated stories, excessive detail, or analytic depth that even interested viewers might not follow; strive for clarity to minimize audience effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity is a central production goal; editors weigh how much detail is appropriate for their perceived audience's attention and comprehension. Anti-pattern: dense, jargon-filled reporting that loses the uninterested majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect from shock (avoid unnecessary personal upset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Television journalists especially guard viewers from unnecessary personal upset; e.g., delaying reporting of a plane crash until a flight number is known to prevent needless worry among viewers with relatives on that flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because viewers cannot 'go back over' a broadcast, producers self-censor or delay to prevent causing undue distress or false hope (e.g., cautious handling of medical-advance stories). Example: withholding a report until confirming identifying details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid provoking panic
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure coverage to discourage public panic in the wake of disasters, assassinations, civil disturbance, or rumor, and to reduce the spread of alarming unverified information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms take pains (especially local stations) to allay fears and avoid speculative reporting that could inflame crowds or cause social disorder. Anti-pattern: sensational live coverage that amplifies rumor or provokes mass anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize imitative behavior (avoid copycat risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publicizing details or imagery that could encourage imitation of harmful acts (e.g., publicity given to would-be assassins or glamorizing criminal acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may refuse covers or prominent placement that could inspire copycats; example: criticism for putting Lynette Fromme on magazine covers after her assassination attempt. Consideration extends to the depiction of subcultures in ways that might romanticize dangerous behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste taboos and content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply taste-based taboos to exclude or edit material involving nudity, profanity, sacrilege, graphic bloodshed, disrespect to certain public institutions (the presidency, wars, patriotism), and (increasingly) racial, religious, and sexual stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste functions to protect both audiences (especially children) and the news organization from backlash. Television is more restrictive (dinner-hour viewing, children present) than magazines; e.g., nudity mostly censored on TV, profanity historically limited, blood and grisly scenes usually omitted. Political taboos (disrespect to the president) often invite protest; personal deviant behavior of officials is treated cautiously and generally only reported if it affects public duties. Standards evolve: some profanity and photo use have relaxed over time, while taboos against stereotypes expanded after criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium- and time-specific constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that format and scheduling (television evening news vs. magazines) impose different restrictions and expectations — e.g., evening TV is constrained by family viewing and affiliate sensitivities, while magazines can occasionally publish nudes or more analytical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must tailor content to the medium's norms and regulatory/affiliate pressures; what is acceptable in a magazine may be unusable on broadcast television. Example: networks avoid erotic depictions and profanity during prime-time broadcasts; magazines have more leeway but still negotiate taboos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect social order / avoid incitement of disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit reporting that could encourage public disorder, spectator attraction to local disturbances, or national diffusion of riots and unrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National media worry about amplifying local disturbances into national contagion (e.g., coverage of 1967 ghetto disorders). Local outlets historically downplay local civil unrest to avoid drawing crowds. This consideration is weighed against the public interest in reporting disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience receptivity as planning criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize the perceived receptivity of the audience to particular material — i.e., whether the (imagined) audience will attend to, accept, and understand the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the main characteristic journalists keep in mind when they do think about the audience: selection and editing aim to match stories to the audience's presumed willingness and capacity to receive them. Risks: conflating journalists' own tastes with audience tastes ('if it bores me, it will bore them').

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and managerial pressures (audience enlargement / cultural democratization tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: News policy must balance journalistic autonomy with corporate profitability: management may push for cost-cutting or more profitable content (celebrity, gossip) to enlarge or change the audience profile, potentially shifting tone and substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be aware that economic pressures can drive content toward wider, less elite audiences (cultural democratization) or more entertainment-oriented formats; this may improve ratings or revenue but risks 'downward mobility' in taste and professional standards. Example: imitation of People magazine's gossip model or format innovations at ABC in response to ratings.
